title: Holy time, not holy place
hook: Shabbat is built in time; it begins at sundown on Friday and ends at nightfall Saturday

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mishkan, a dwelling built from everyone's gifts, and the end of camp two. Your line was build a place, presence comes. Today camp three begins: the practices.

People cross oceans to stand somewhere holy. A cathedral. A mountaintop. A shrine at the end of a long road. Jewish tradition also keeps a holy place you don't travel to at all, because it travels to you. It arrives every week, on the same day, wherever you are: a hospital room, a dorm, a kitchen in a small apartment. You can't buy a ticket to it, and you can't be too far away from it. It just comes, at sundown, on Friday.
screen: `HOLY PLACES YOU TRAVEL TO.` → `A HOLY PLACE THAT COMES TO YOU.` → `EVERY FRIDAY, AT SUNDOWN.`

segments.voice: Go back to the first chapters of Genesis. God makes light, sky, sea, land, stars, animals and people, and calls them good. But the first thing the Torah calls holy isn't any of them. It's a day. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Hallowed means made holy, kadosh in Hebrew. Before there was a holy mountain or a holy tent, there was a holy time. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel built a whole book on that observation. He described Shabbat as a sanctuary built in time instead of in space, a palace people enter once a week and leave at the end of the day. Yesterday's mishkan was a tent you could carry. Shabbat is even more portable. The Jewish day starts in the evening, because Genesis says there was evening and there was morning. So Shabbat begins at sundown on Friday. Candles are lit a little before sunset, and it ends on Saturday night when three stars can be seen in the sky. A little more than a full day. In that time, observant Jews stop the kind of work that makes and changes the world, and spend the day on rest, meals, prayer, family, study and friends. Others keep parts of it: a Friday dinner, candles, an unplugged afternoon. Jewish movements differ on how Shabbat is kept, and Jews find their own places on that range. What they share is the idea underneath: some things can't be made in space. They can only be kept in time.
screen: `THE FIRST HOLY THING WAS A DAY.` · `A PALACE IN TIME.` · `SUNDOWN FRIDAY TO THREE STARS.` · `KEPT IN MANY WAYS.` · then, large: `AND GOD BLESSED THE SEVENTH DAY.`

segments.voice: Look at the week ahead like a calendar on the wall, and find one hour, Friday night, Saturday afternoon, or any hour that works for your life, to spend without producing, fixing, buying or posting anything. Picture it: where you'd be, who'd be there, what you'd do instead. Then mark it, in your head or in your phone.
Holy time. Shabbat, the first thing the Torah calls holy: a day, not a place, from sundown Friday to nightfall Saturday.
Your line: a palace in time. You don't travel to it; it comes to you. Day ninety-seven, done.

howItsDone: Shabbat begins at sundown on Friday and ends when three stars appear on Saturday night; many Jewish families mark it with candles, a festive meal and a day set apart from work.

chat.says: Why do people call Shabbat "a palace in time"?
options: The first thing the Torah calls holy is a day, not a place, and it comes to you.
Because the Temple was finished on a Saturday, so the day took its name.
Because Shabbat is only holy inside a synagogue, at set prayer times.
chat.meaning: God blessed the seventh day and made it holy before any holy mountain or tent. Heschel called Shabbat a sanctuary built in time.
